cases.title: Puerto Varas case: unlocking commercial potential on rural land | Land Advisors
cases.description: Puerto Varas case study: land with a commercial use restriction, a market intelligence read of connectivity and town growth, and an estimated +50% value capture over purchase price.
cases.h1: From a use restriction to commercial potential
cases.intro: A property near Puerto Varas carried an explicit commercial use prohibition in its listing. The market set it aside; our read of access, growth, and zoning identified a different opportunity.
cases.author: José Hernán Katz C.
cases.imageAlt: Puerto Varas and the Lago Llanquihue shoreline

ila.thesisMarket: The market read the listing's commercial use prohibition as the end of the conversation.
ila.thesisTerritory: Connectivity, adjacent urbanization, and corridor trajectory pointed to commercial potential the listing did not convey.

sections.text: What the market saw

The buyer sought land with commercial potential on rural land near Puerto Varas. The listing showed a strong location, but the documentation included an explicit commercial use restriction—enough for most prospective buyers to set the property aside.
What we identified

We evaluated real connectivity rather than map distance, traffic on the corridor, the growth trajectory of the sector, and the property's zoning history. The restriction existed on paper, but the local context—access improvements, adjacent urbanization, and municipal investment near town—pointed to commercial potential the listing did not convey.

items: Connectivity and real travel times to town services
Zoning and planning rules applicable to the property
Comparable sales for land with a similar highest and best use

sections.text: Acquisition strategy

With verifiable information, the buyer moved forward with a clear view of the regulatory risk and the path to lifting the restriction. The decision rested on the relationship between entry price, highest and best use, and negotiation margin—rather than on how the land looked in photos.
Result
Following the required process, the commercial use prohibition was lifted. Estimated value capture was approximately 50% above the purchase price.
What this means for buyers

A listing restriction can conceal an opportunity—provided zoning and local market conditions are evaluated before making an offer. The reverse also holds: land that appears unrestricted on paper can prove costly when site preparation and infrastructure costs or connectivity do not support the project.
Past results do not guarantee future results. Illustrative case with aggregated data. Does not constitute personalized advice or a promise of returns.

faq.q: Can a commercial use restriction always be lifted?
faq.a: Not always. The outcome depends on the property, the current planning instrument, and the applicable procedure—each case calls for regulatory verification before assuming a path to lifting the restriction.

faq.q: Why did the market pass on this land?
faq.a: A visible prohibition in a listing acts as an automatic filter. Few buyers go on to evaluate connectivity, town growth, and local comparable sales—the full assessment that revealed this opportunity.

faq.q: Did Land Advisors sell this land?
faq.a: No. We are an independent land advisory firm, not a brokerage or listing portal. We support the purchase decision with market intelligence and local expertise.

cases.title: Frutillar case: positioning through seller dynamics | Land Advisors
cases.description: Frutillar case study: a gap between asking price and market value, a motivated seller, and an acquisition at 26M resold at 42M in two months.
cases.intro: To the market, it was one more lot among the Frutillar listings. Read through seller liquidity and comparable sales, it was an actionable price gap.
cases.author: José Hernán Katz C.
cases.imageAlt: Land in Frutillar, Lago Llanquihue basin

ila.thesisMarket: To the market, it was one more lot in the visible Frutillar supply.
ila.thesisTerritory: The gap lay in seller liquidity and local comparable sales—rather than in future sector appreciation.

sections.text: What the market saw
The buyer was evaluating options in Frutillar within a defined budget. Visible supply included dozens of similar listings—comparable only with local expertise and a clear framework.
What we identified

We measured the asking price against closed sales in the area—beyond active listings—evaluated the sector's highest and best use within rural land near Frutillar, and identified signs of seller urgency: a need for liquidity and a tight timeline.
Acquisition strategy
The acquisition was structured on the verifiable gap between list price and local market value rather than on a future appreciation narrative. The return was built into the transaction itself.
Result
Acquired at 26 million pesos and resold at 42 million in approximately two months, with comparable sales supporting the exit value.
What this means for buyers

Returns do not always depend on waiting years for a sector to transform. Often, value is created at acquisition—by identifying price gaps, seller liquidity, and pricing errors, supported by local comparable sales.
Past results do not guarantee future results. Illustrative case with aggregated data. Does not constitute personalized advice or a promise of returns.

faq.q: Does this type of arbitrage recur in Frutillar?
faq.a: Price gaps emerge where there is information asymmetry or seller urgency. They cannot be replicated on demand: each opportunity calls for local market intelligence and verifiable comparable sales.

faq.q: How do you tell a low price from problematic land?
faq.a: A low price can signal opportunity or risk—access, services, or zoning. The distinction comes from weighing purchase price, site preparation and infrastructure costs, and exit value against local data.

faq.q: Which service fits if I am seeking this type of opportunity?
faq.a: Personalized Search evaluates at least 4 options with local expertise; together, we select the 3 strongest for a comparative report.

cases.title: Llanquihue case: present price vs. long-term value | Land Advisors
cases.description: Llanquihue case study: a partly urbanized project, developer liquidity pressure, and the acquisition of 4 lots for 4,400 UF with a later market reference of ~2,000 UF per lot.
cases.intro: A partly urbanized development can look attractive on unit price. The essential question is whether present value compensates for site preparation risk and timelines.
cases.author: José Hernán Katz C.
cases.imageAlt: Rural land in Llanquihue with development potential

ila.thesisMarket: The price per lot looked competitive against standalone alternatives.
ila.thesisTerritory: The opportunity lay in present value negotiated around developer liquidity—rather than in a distant appreciation promise.

sections.text: What the market saw

The buyer was evaluating a partly urbanized development in Llanquihue. The price per lot looked competitive against standalone alternatives, yet it had not been weighed against pending site preparation and infrastructure costs, real timelines, and exit liquidity.
What we identified

We evaluated urbanization status, services delivered versus promised, subdivision regulations, comparable sales for serviced land in the sector and—critically—the developer's liquidity position, which shaped the negotiation.

items: Status of urbanization works and services
Comparable sales for serviced land in the area
Cost overrun and permitting timeline risk

sections.text: Acquisition strategy

The acquisition was structured on verifiable present value: a negotiated entry price amid seller liquidity pressure, with a conservative post-urbanization value projection—grounded in data rather than project promises.
Result
Acquisition of 4 lots for 4,400 UF in total. Subsequent market reference: approximately 2,000 UF per serviced lot under comparable conditions.
What this means for buyers

In partly urbanized projects, a per-lot price can mask pending costs and timelines. Add purchase price, site preparation, and time—then compare against a conservative sale scenario rather than the developer's brochure.
Past results do not guarantee future results. Illustrative case with aggregated data. Does not constitute personalized advice or a promise of returns.

faq.q: Is it worth buying in a partly urbanized subdivision?
faq.a: It can be, when present value is supported by verifiable comparable sales and pending costs are quantified. When the price already reflects unsupported future value, risk increases.

faq.q: What should I review in the co-ownership bylaws?
faq.a: Permitted uses, building restrictions, pending urbanization fees, and management rules. In subdivisions, these can limit cabins, retail, or density.

faq.q: Does Land Advisors recommend specific projects?
faq.a: We evaluate each option against your objective and recommend with data—including when the right move is to keep searching. We have no land or projects of our own to sell.
